content: The process of determining the direction and strength of each intervention was conducted in two stages. Initially, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) evaluated all domains included in the evidence-to-decision framework. These domains encompassed benefits versus risks, certainty of evidence, values and preferences, acceptability, feasibility, resource use, and equity issues. Based on this evaluation, the GDG decided whether to (1) recommend in favor, (2) recommend against, or (3) make no recommendation. The strength of a recommendation reflected the GDG's confidence that the desirable effects outweighed the undesirable effects. Desirable effects included improved health outcomes, such as reduced HIV incidence, morbidity, and mortality, as well as decreased burdens on individuals and health services, and potential cost savings for individuals, communities, programs, and health systems. Undesirable effects included potential harms to individuals, families, communities, or health services, as well as resource use and cost implications. A conditional recommendation was made when the GDG concluded that the desirable effects of adherence to the recommendation probably outweighed the undesirable effects or were closely balanced, but there was uncertainty about these trade-offs in all situations. Implementation of such recommendations required monitoring and rigorous evaluation to address uncertainties, potentially generating new evidence that could alter the balance of trade-offs and suggest ways to overcome implementation challenges. The GDG reached consensus on the wording and strength of each recommendation, with all members agreeing on the formulation and providing vocal approval during meetings. Systematic reviews of evidence were guided by PICO questions formulated by the WHO Steering Group. A Systematic Review Team developed protocols and conducted reviews, adhering to PRISMA guidelines for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Data from these reviews were summarized as evidence profiles using the GRADE approach. The GDG reviewed outputs generated by an individual-based simulation model (HIV synthesis model) of HIV transmission, progression, and the effects of antiretroviral therapy (ART), including the impact of drug-resistant virus acquisition and transmission. This model, previously used to address questions related to HIV and ART programs, was employed to assess the impact of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) on mortality, HIV incidence, and program costs. Parameters such as ART adherence, interruption rates, and switching to second-line ART after first-line failure were varied within plausible bounds for specific geographical regions. The model focused on heterosexual HIV transmission in adult populations in sub-Saharan Africa and did not include children or mother-to-child transmission of HIVDR. Outcomes for each policy option were generated every three months and averaged over a 20-year period (2018–2038). The GDG also considered acceptability, values, and preferences of end-users, including people living with HIV, program managers, clinicians, and other healthcare workers. Evidence was gathered through online surveys, expert meetings, and consultations with health ministries, program managers, implementing partners, and donors across WHO regions. These findings informed discussions on the feasibility of proposed interventions. The GDG met in Geneva, Switzerland, in March 2017 to review evidence, formulate recommendations, and develop a consensus statement. Discussions were facilitated by a methodologist, and systematic review results included GRADE evidence profile tables for outcome data. The group reached consensus on thresholds for pre-treatment HIVDR to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) that would trigger public health responses. This involved reviewing prevalence data, systematic reviews, modeling data, and the acceptability and feasibility of interventions. The group agreed on the necessity of a consensus statement to guide country-level decisions, the public health responses to be triggered, and the quantitative thresholds for pre-treatment HIVDR. An external review group, selected to ensure geographical and gender balance and broad expertise, reviewed a draft of the guidelines and provided comments via an online platform. This process allowed for transparent, real-time commenting and responses. The WHO Steering Group reviewed all comments and resolved disagreements, ensuring that specific changes were made to the guidelines in response to feedback. Conflicts of interest were managed rigorously. All contributors, including GDG and external review group members, completed WHO declarations of interest forms. The WHO Steering Group reviewed these forms and conducted online searches for potential conflicts, focusing on the use of antiretroviral drugs and laboratory assays for detecting HIVDR. Significant conflicts of interest were identified for two candidates, who were excluded from the GDG. No significant conflicts were identified for GDG members who attended the meeting. Declared interests were shared with all participants, and the co-chairs and WHO Steering Group ensured that all members could express their views without undue influence. A systematic review assessing the prevalence of pre-treatment HIVDR from 1993 to 2016 across 63 lowand middle-income countries showed an increase in pre-treatment HIVDR over time. The annual incremental increase in pre-treatment HIVDR to NNRTIs varied by region, with the highest rates observed in eastern and southern Africa. WHO surveys typically measured pre-treatment HIVDR among all individuals starting first-line ART, including ARV drug-naïve initiators, those with prior ARV drug exposure, and those reinitiating ART after previous treatment. In most lowand middle-income countries, NNRTI-based first-line ART was administered regardless of prior ARV drug exposure, reflecting programmatic realities. Of 11 countries reporting nationally representative survey data between 2014 and 2016, six had pre-treatment HIVDR prevalence to NNRTIs exceeding 10%, and two exceeded 15%. Countries with lower prevalence estimates often monitored pre-treatment HIVDR only in ARV drug-naïve individuals, potentially underestimating the true prevalence. Pre-treatment HIVDR to NNRTIs was significantly higher among previously exposed ART initiators compared to ARV drug-naïve individuals.
